1.pericope_label: Naomi's counsel: the kinsman, the threshing-floor, and the uncovering of the feet

schools.summary: Lay down the land law the chapter turns on, that under the theocratic constitution the land belonged to God and the possessor held only the usufruct, so that the family portion could not be sold at will but was to remain for ever in the family, from which it follows that the request was a claim the law already recognised; brush aside a word added to the text as unnecessary; take the motives to include the fear that the mother-in-law's own death would leave her companion unprotected; press the second clause as meaning that marriage must be for the good and comfort and abiding peace not of the body only but of the soul; render the gesture literally as lifting the clothes that lie on the feet, and report the surviving custom of owners sleeping on their threshing-floors with their feet covered by a mantle.

Commend both motives — justice to the dead, that seed might be raised up and the family not made extinct, and gratitude to a daughter-in-law who had behaved dutifully; observe that one who had resolved on perpetual widowhood herself was far from confining a young woman to it, since age must not make itself a standard to youth, and that she projected for her daughter what the daughter's modesty forbade her to project for herself; draw from the word rest that a married state is or should be a state of rest to the young, wandering affections being then fixed; and admit that the course taken was very extraordinary and looks suspicious, the fault, if there was anything improper in it, lying on the one who knew the laws and usages of Israel better.

Say plainly that the experiment was dangerous and should in no sense be imitated, since had the man not been of extraordinary piety, prudence and continence it might have been fatal, and that the mother-in-law probably knew more than she revealed; make the gesture a marital usage, women in the East going to the bed's foot and gently raising the clothes to creep under them, or else read it simply as a device to wake him; describe the winnowing as letting the corn fall slowly in the wind so the grain drops by its weight and the chaff is carried off, and explain the hour by the evening sea breeze; and add that the floor was covered overhead but open at the sides, the work usually ending with a feast.

Keep to the ground of the claim, that the man was thought the next nearest kinsman and so obliged by the law to marry her; and take the washing and the raiment as meant to make her clean and neat and free from any disagreeable aspect, so as to be the better received.

debates: What Naomi intended by the advice, and for whose sake.
Whether the means she chose were proper.
What the uncovering of the feet consisted in and signified.
Why the winnowing was done at night.
outliers: Keil alone supplies the land law that turns the request into a legal claim.
Clarke alone calls the experiment dangerous and says it should in no sense be imitated.
Henry alone says that if anything was improper the fault must lie on Naomi rather than on Ruth.
Clarke alone explains the night winnowing by the sea breeze that set in at evening.
Ellicott alone reports the surviving custom of sleeping on the threshing-floor with the feet under a mantle.

5.pericope_label: Ruth goes down to the floor, and Boaz wakes at midnight

schools.summary: Ground the compliance on the young woman's judgment of her mother-in-law, of whose piety and prudence she had the highest opinion, being confident she would never advise what was contrary to religion and virtue; report the Chaldee addition that the man blessed the Lord who had heard his prayer and taken the famine away; note that the eating and drinking was free but not to excess, innocent mirth having always been allowed in harvest and vintage; and explain the sleeping from the dress, since long garments served to sleep in by night as well as to cover by day, and it was not thought unworthy of persons of note to lie so.

Call the obedience an intelligent obedience, since she knew the relation in which the man stood to her family and the duties attaching to it, so that her trust is implicit but not blind and she risks obloquy in conscious innocence; and describe the waking exactly, the word meaning startled rather than afraid and the verb being literally to bend oneself, so that he starts awake, bends forward to feel who is there, and sees a woman at his feet.

Treat the whole scene as a lesson in household management: the master was with his servants at the winnowing and had his eye on them, not against theft but against waste, since masters may lose much by servants heedless though honest; he gave extraordinary entertainment when there was extraordinary work and ate with them, it well becoming the rich and great to be generous to and familiar with those under them; he kept good hours, so that by midnight he had already had his first sleep; and he lay at the corn-heap not from covetousness but because it was too late to go home and he would be near his work, showing besides that he was no more nice in his lodging than the patriarch who could make his bed in a barn; then build on the Chaldee addition, that he went sober to bed with his heart in a good frame and did not go to bed without prayer, which was well, since he had an unusual temptation before him and knew nothing of it.

Suppose that since threshing-floors in the East are in the open air the owner or a trusted man stayed in the fields till the grain was secured, keeping a tent at the place; report how much trouble the verb gave the old paraphrast, who made the man tremble till his flesh was like a boiled turnip, and how that paraphrast went on to compare his self-command with two other examples of continence; draw from the verse that he had no intimation whatever of what was in hand; and dispose of the hour by saying only that he did not discover her sooner.

debates: On what ground Ruth complied with the advice.
Why Boaz slept at the heap of corn.
What weight the Chaldee additions carry.
What the verb rendered turned himself describes.
outliers: Henry alone reads the scene as a lesson in the management of a household.
Ellicott alone calls the obedience intelligent rather than blind, and has her risk obloquy in conscious innocence.
Clarke alone reports the paraphrast's simile of the boiled turnip and his comparison with two other examples of continence.
Gill alone explains the long garment that served for clothing by day and bedding by night.
Clarke alone supposes a tent kept standing at the threshing-floor.

9.pericope_label: Spread thy skirt over thine handmaid: the claim made, and a nearer kinsman

schools.summary: Take the figure of the wing from the young of fowls running under their mothers for shelter from birds of prey, so that the words mean simply, take me to thee for wife, and report that a Jew to this day throws the skirt of his garment over his bride to signify that he has taken her under his protection; confess that the praise is not easy to make out, and read the word we translate kindness as piety, so that the later act proves her sincerity better than her becoming a proselyte could, and infer that she did not seek the marriage to mend her condition, since she might have had a rich young man; suppose a brother of the dead man's father still living, with the prior right, and note that the mother-in-law very likely knew nothing of it.

Deny that the figure is taken from birds covering their young and refer it to the corner of the counterpane which a man spreads over his wife, or else hold both senses at once, giving the literal wing, reporting that the old paraphrast made the words themselves a claim to espousal, and illustrating from the prophet who uses the image of marriage and the gospel image of a bird gathering her brood; note that the word stands as a dual but is most probably a singular; divide the two kindnesses, the earlier shown to the dead husband and the mother-in-law, the later in not going after young men as young women generally do but turning to an older man that her husband might have a successor; read the blessing as sufficient proof of the view he took of her conduct and of his own integrity, following as it does immediately on her giving her name; and note that the city is literally the gate, the meeting-place of those going in and out.

Mark the manner of the reply, that instead of calling her immodest for lying at his feet, or bold for asking marriage when she was poor, or being angry at being frightened out of sleep, he blesses her and calls her his daughter; spell out the three things she was told not to fear — being forced and defiled, being reproached afterwards as immodest, and being despised as poor and failing in her suit; and make the kinship close and simple, the dead husband and this man having been the sons of brothers.

debates: Whether the figure of the wing is drawn from birds or from the marriage bed.
What the two kindnesses were, and what the word for kindness means.
What Ruth was being told not to fear.
In what degree Boaz stood related, and who the nearer kinsman was.
outliers: Keil alone denies the bird metaphor and refers the wing to the corner of the counterpane.
Clarke alone reports the surviving custom of throwing the skirt of the garment over the bride.
Clarke alone confesses the praise hard to make out, and reads the word for kindness as piety.
Ellicott alone takes the answer as proof of the integrity of both parties at once.
Gill alone enumerates the three distinct fears the reassurance is meant to meet.

13.pericope_label: Tarry until the morning: the secrecy, the six measures, and the waiting at home

schools.summary: Have him grant that her plea is clear and assented to while forbidding the risk of a journey in the dead of night; quote the puritan expositor by name for the rule that we must keep not only a good conscience but a good name, and avoid not only sin but scandal, and note that the word is the woman, this woman, so that his thought is of her and not himself; raise the point that the verb is masculine in the current Hebrew, so that it should read he went, the old paraphrast marking the distinction by supplying the man's name, though many manuscripts with the Syriac and Latin take it as feminine and the Greek cannot show the difference — on which reading he goes to the city to find the nearer kinsman while she goes home; take the question at the door as asking in what circumstances she comes, that is, what she has accomplished, or how she has fared; and note that the phrase about the matter falling rests on the image of a lot falling to the ground.

Say that the lodging was for her safety and honour and from no design upon her; report that the first letter of the word for tarry is written larger than usual, which some take as a mark to fix the reader's attention on so singular a thing as a widow lodging with a man without any diminution of her chastity, and and close with the counsel that she keep at home, say nothing of the affair to anyone, and be easy about it until the issue is known.

Quote an earlier bishop's summary entire, that instead of touching her as a wanton he blessed her as a father, encouraged her as a friend, promised her as a kinsman, rewarded her as a patron, and sent her away laden with hopes and gifts, no less chaste but more happy than she came; note that the Hebrew names no quantity for the measures, and reason from the paraphrast's own added blessing that he felt the larger reckoning too heavy a load for a woman, where the smaller makes a goodly present and no miracle; read the question at the door as wonder rather than doubt; and observe that no time was lost in bringing the matter to an issue.

Note that she lay at his feet and not by his side, and went as soon as there was light, before one could know another, being unashamed of the mark of her poverty but unwilling to be known abroad at night, her virtue being her greatest honour; be frank about the charge of secrecy, that though both were conscious of an unspotted purity few could come so near the fire without being scorched, so that discovery would have raised suspicions in some and reflections from others, troubling good people and giving bad people a triumph; add the practical reason, that if the matter took wind it might prejudice the other kinsman's freedom of choice; and take the gift as evidence that she was not sent away in dislike, given by measure like a prudent corn-master keeping account of what he delivered out.

debates: Why the night's lodging had to be kept secret.
What quantity the six measures amounted to.
Whether the verb at the close of the fifteenth verse is masculine or feminine, and who went where.
What Naomi meant by asking who she was.
outliers: Ellicott alone raises the masculine verb and the divergence of the versions over it.
Clarke alone reasons from the paraphrast's added blessing that he felt the weight of the larger measure.
Gill alone reports the enlarged letter in the Hebrew text and the marks that have been connected with it.
Wesley alone quotes an earlier writer's summary of the whole encounter.
Henry alone gives the practical reason for secrecy, that discovery would have prejudiced the other kinsman's choice.
